newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Pick 'n Pay to focus on financial services.
newsitem.headline: Pick 'n Pay to focus on financial services.

text.p: A major move into targeted financial services and the refurbishment of stores would be the priorities for Pick 'n Pay Stores Ltd over the next year, the group said on Wednesday.
Releasing record results for the year to February 28, chairman Raymond Ackerman and managing directors Gareth Ackerman and Sean Summers predicted steady growth this year despite a tight market.
The group beat most predictions by announcing a 30 percent rise in headline earnings to 29.33 cents from 22.55 cents and a dividend of 22.80 cents compared to 13.50 cents last year.
Gareth Ackerman said the move into financial services would be "the major thrust for Pick 'n Pay for this year".

"It is going to take us a while to get it up and running but the profit contribution of financial services, looking two three years into the future, we believe is going to be considerable and will provide a valuable extension to the Pick 'n Pay brand in the market place."
The group recently announced that the contract for the launch into financial services had been awarded to Boland Bank. Ackerman said that further details would be announced soon.
This was not a completely new departure for the group, but would consolidate financial services already being offered into a cohesive package, Ackerman said.
The company already offers a credit card to about 50,000 customers and a debit card to 20,000 people.

The group also runs Transwitch Services, which allows customers to pay for their shopping and draw cash at Pick'n Pay stores. It accepts cards from all banks apart from First National Bank and Nedbank, who have refused to join the scheme.
"We suddenly realised that we have been in the financial services game, but not really with a major product," Ackerman said.
"It will probably be a card based product but the details of that product we are not releasing right now for obvious competitive reasons."
Services offered by several U.K. stores included savings programmes, unit trust schemes and long term insurance policies for education and medical benefits.
"Potential products that we could look at are funeral benefit products," Ackerman said.

"One has to look at products that are going to be easy for consumers to understand, easy to source. The fundamental issue is that we will not be a manufacturer. We will be a distributor of products. We are out in the market place looking for the best provider of a particular product that we will design."
Summers said that the refurbishment of stores, which had started with the Norwood hypermarket, had shown good results and would be continued this year.
This had involved a major move into the fresh food and perishables market, which had improved margins.
Raymond Ackerman said the restructuring of the group over the last year into two separate divisions had had its problems but appeared to be working well.
"We see the company in the next three to five years as being in a fairly strong growth phase, but it has got to be done in a very planned and managed fashion," Gareth Ackerman said.
